messages.subject: logit MEMs and categorical variables
messages.body_plain:
Some colleagues and I are working with linear mixed effects models (with empirical logit transforms for proportion data) with categorical variables and have some questions regarding interpretation.

For a sample of what we're dealing with, let's assume we want to look at whether a participant's response (correct/incorrect) is affected by a stimulus cue, and there are three (non-ordinal) categories of cues: match, mismatch, and neutral.


1.       Contrast coding: if we were doing this with ANOVA and found a main effect, we'd then do pairwise t-tests to determine how the three conditions differed from each other.  Most of the reading I've done (including here http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/r/library/contrast_coding.htm) don't seem to want to let us look at all pairwise comparisons- we can only compare two of them to a reference level (compare match to neutral and mismatch to neutral, but not match to mismatch.)  To get around this, we've been running the model with different categories set as the reference level, which is an ok hack with just 3 categories- but some of our studies have more than three levels and it just seems inefficient.   Is there a better way to do this, or a reason we definitely SHOULDN'T be doing this?



2.       Can mixed effect models take the place of t-tests comparing proportion correct to chance levels?  One of our studies has multiple stimulus categories (eight, actually) and we are trying to determine if participants are above chance on a 2AFC decision for each category. We have arbitrarily picked one reference category and see a significant intercept, which we're interpreting as reliable above-chance accuracy for that category. There are no significant coefficients for the rest of the fixed effect levels, which we're interpreting as all the other 7 categories are also being reliably mapped to their correct meanings (because they're not reliably different from the intercept). Before we ran this model, we had reported t-tests comparing proportion correct for each word to 0.5. Does the mixed effects model replace these?



3.     We're trying to find other papers that have reported using logit mixed effects models with categorical predictors so that we can see what others have done and how they've reported it.  Can anyone recommend a recent paper that has used these techniques appropriately and explained the results well?


Thanks,
- Kate


Kate Pirog Revill, PhD
FERN Facilities Manager/Sr. Research Scientist
Emory University

messages.subject: Re: logit MEMs and categorical variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kate,

> 1.Contrast coding: if we were doing this with ANOVA and found a main 
> effect, we'd then do pairwise t-tests to determine how the three 
> conditions differed from each other.  Most of the reading I've done 
> (including here 
> http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/r/library/contrast_coding.htm 
> <http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/r/library/contrast_coding.htm>) don't 
> seem to want to let us look at all pairwise comparisons- we can only 
> compare two of them to a reference level (compare match to neutral and 
> mismatch to neutral, but not match to mismatch.)  To get around this, 
> we've been running the model with different categories set as the 
> reference level, which is an ok hack with just 3 categories- but some 
> of our studies have more than three levels and it just seems 
> inefficient.  Is there a better way to do this, or a reason we 
> definitely SHOULDN'T be doing this?
>

In general, I find that when you have a 3+ level categorical predictor 
dummy coding often leads to models that are considerably easier to 
interpret. The way that I would typically do the sorts of pairwise 
comparisons that you're interested in is by analysing specific subsets 
of the data. Assuming the 3 level predictor is dummy coded, in your full 
model you'll have an intercept,  which is the mean for the, e.g., 
neutral condition, one slope showing the difference between means for 
the match and the neutral conditions and a second slope showing the 
difference between the means of the mismatch and neutral conditions. If 
you then delete the neutral cases, you can compare match vs. mismatch 
directly. g/lmer() has a subset option to allow just this sort of thing.

There's no reason why you couldn't relevel the predictor (e.g. taking 
match as a baseline to get match vs. neutral and match vs. mismatch) but 
when it comes time to write up the results you probably don't want to 
report two models which are identical save for the fact that one is 
coded differently to the other.


> 2.Can mixed effect models take the place of t-tests comparing 
> proportion correct to chance levels?  One of our studies has multiple 
> stimulus categories (eight, actually) and we are trying to determine 
> if participants are above chance on a 2AFC decision for each 
> category. We have arbitrarily picked one reference category and see a 
> significant intercept, which we're interpreting as reliable 
> above-chance accuracy for that category. There are no significant 
> coefficients for the rest of the fixed effect levels, which we're 
> interpreting as all the other 7 categories are also being reliably 
> mapped to their correct meanings (because they're not reliably 
> different from the intercept). Before we ran this model, we had 
> reported t-tests comparing proportion correct for each word to 0.5. 
> Does the mixed effects model replace these?
>

I don't really have much to add here, but I might be a little cautious 
about inferring that all of the categories are above chance on the basis 
of this one model. It seems possible to me that while the grand mean 
(which is what the intercept represents when you use contrast coding) 
will significantly differ from zero at least one condition would not. 
One or more conditions will almost certainly be numerically less than 
the grand mean. Imagine that the grand mean is 1. The slope for 
condition A is -0.2, and so the mean for condition A will be 0.8. While 
1 may be significantly different from 0, it's not out-with the realm of 
possibility that 0.8 isn't. You do occassionally see head-scratching 
cases of three-level predictors where A < B, A = C, but, according to 
p-values, B = C.

The most rigorous way to do a mixed effect version of the one sample 
t-test you mention is to subset the data for a single condition, and 
then build a regression model containing only the intercept (and random 
intercepts). In that model the intercept would tell you the mean for 
that condition. You would have to do it 8 times, and any condition which 
didn't have a significant intercept could not be said to be above (or 
below) chance.

With that said, if I wanted to find out whether people were performing 
above chance then I'd calculate 95% confidence intervals (1.96 * SE) for 
the proportions in each condition and just check that they didn't 
overlap with 0.5. It'sa much more flexible solution than relying 
regression intercepts, since there may be cases where chance isn't .5.

HTH,

Ian

messages.subject: Re: logit MEMs and categorical variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kate,
Regarding the pairwise t-tests, Scott Jackson gave a very nice explanation
of how to use the "multcomp" package to do this on this list a few years
ago, so I will just point to his answer(s):
General case:
http://pidgin.ucsd.edu/pipermail/r-lang/mailman.ucsd.edu/pipermail/ling-r-lang-l/2012-October/000381.html
Longitudinal case:
http://pidgin.ucsd.edu/pipermail/r-lang/mailman.ucsd.edu/pipermail/ling-r-lang-l/2012-November/000393.html

I'm pretty sure that a carefully constructed contrast matrix could also be
used to test whether any of the individual factor levels are different from
chance. An easier option might be to use the "effects" package, which
should give you point estimates and confidence intervals for each factor
level. Just guessing at your data, I think something like this would work:

as.data.frame(effect("Category", m))

Where Category is the name of the stimulus categories factor and m is the
fitted model from (g)lmer.

Hope that helps,
Dan

messages.subject: Re: logit MEMs and categorical variables
messages.body_plain:
"The way that I would typically do the sorts of pairwise comparisons that
you're interested in is by analysing specific subsets of the data."

I had a question about this, and please bear in mind that I do not have a
real background in statistics! From an ANOVA point of view, my
understanding is that the above recommendation is not kosher. If it was,
then why would statisticians have developed the post-hoc tests that are
typically used? At the least, one is told to establish an overall
significance (F-test) before any discussion of pairwise comparisons, and
when the latter are made, you may need to worry about multiple comparisons
corrections anyway.

What I was wondering i about a situation or experiment where you have a
clear baseline-treatment setup, but you have two treatments. To my mind,
taking something you're considering a baseline measurement from subjects,
and then measuring two separate treatment effects, is sort of like "two
experiments in one". And if you're interested in T1 vs. T2, I would think
it's a better design than running two separate experiments.

But whether you're looking at T1 vs. T2, or if you're only interested in B
vs. T1 and B vs. T2, is it OK to simply hide the third category and use a
binary predictor? It is not easy for me to see why doing so is bad. Maybe
it's not, I was just confused by the similarity to ANOVA where skipping
ahead to pairwise comparisons is not done.

Thanks,
Dan
